chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text:
Matt Joras said:

I think that can be provided by the Android folks, however I'm not sure that we should base decisions on working on a protocol mechanism on the API decisions of a platform.

Not so much to make a decision here, but to ensure that the API is fit for purpose.  Not an IETF thing as much as someone who has a stake in shipping a QUIC stack that works well on Android.

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: I believe the Android platform can supply the token to the application, rather than the reverse.  That would limit an application's ability to make the platform send arbitrary packets at shutdown.  (I still don't know why that capability would be a problem though.)

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: A complete API might need to give the OS information about which UDP packets trigger a response (to supply the incoming CID) and then information on what packet to send back.  To @Benjamin Schwartz's point, which is a good one, you could give the OS control over the token.  But the DCID of that packet will be under application control.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: Of course, the application can send arbitrary UDP packets in this setting, so having the OS send a more narrowly-scoped thing in response is strictly less capable.  So maybe this is not something to worry about.

The Transport-Info header provides a mechanism to transmit network transport related information such as current delivery rate and round-trip time, from a server or a client.
